newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: INSTANT VIEW-Australian wages, building approvals.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW-Australian wages, building approvals.

text.p: Australian average weekly ordinary time earnings (AWOTE) rose 1.3 percent in the three months to February to be 4.6 percent higher over the previous 12 months, official figures showed.
Market forecasts had centred on a 0.8 percent quarterly increase and annual wages growth of 4.3 percent.
Seperate data showed that building approvals fell 1.8 percent in March, against median expectations of a 2.0 percent rise.
A selection of economists' immediate reactions to the data follows.
JOHN EDWARDS, CHIEF ECONOMIST, HSBC MARKETS:
"Whatever reservations there might be about the accuracy of the (wages) number, it rules out a rate cut next week (when the RBA holds its monthly board meeting)."
DAVID BASSENESE, SENIOR ECONOMIST, BANKERS TRUST:

"I wouldn't get overly concerned with that (wages) number. The headline number is clearly stronger than we had been thinking. If we look at the private/public sector split, which we will get down the track (May 22), that's the key because this number could be boosted by the distortions that are going on in the public sector due to layoffs."
STEPHEN KOUKOULAS, CHIEF ECONOMIST, CITIBANK AUSTRALIA:

"It must be a real concern to the policy makers that we are getting such wage outcomes when the labour market is so weak. Maybe there is a bit more to the wage negotiations than we first thought. It means rates are not going to be cut here in a hurry. Obviously, there's more to interest rates than wages but they get a big weighting and these sorts of figures are a concern."
ROB HENDERSON, CHIEF ECONOMIST, DRESDNER AUSTRALIA:

"Well they're pretty disappointing after all of the good news we've had on the wages and inflation outlook over the last couple of weeks. These numbers may be influenced by the compositional effect in the public sector, and let's hope that's the case. But at this point in time you'd have to say that certainly a number like 4.6 percent is too high to be comfortable for the Reserve Bank, so basically forget any prospect of another cut in interest rates until it becomes clear that this is not a sign of accelerating wages growth."
IVAN COLHOUN, ASSOCIATE DIRECTOR, DEUTSCHE MORGAN GRENFELL:

"Wages were certainly a surprise for the market, they were certainly above expectations. Even though it is historical it would be higher than the Reserve Bank has previously assessed wages as growing. It might explain why employment growth has been soft. The market said it diminishes the chance of a rate cut, and I guess the first impact is that that is the correct call. I think they (the RBA) will be looking at some of the other indicators and not totally ruling it out."
NIGEL STAPLEDON, ECONOMIST, WESTPAC BANKING CORP:

"It's not a good result, but I'm not going to panic on that. I would see it as more of a statistical correction to some abberantly good numbers (particularly on private sector wages). I don't see in these numbers a genuine upward trend in wages growth. It does no more than confirm our view that there's no (monetary policy) change on the agenda at present. There's no possibility that the RBA will ease. Monetary policy is going to stay on hold into the middle of next year."
